newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak January trade deficit more than trebles.
newsitem.headline: Slovak January trade deficit more than trebles.

text.p: Slovakia's January foreign trade deficit more than trebled to 7.061 billion crowns on increased imports of fossil fuels, nuclear plant technology and cars, the Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said on Tuesday.
The January trade deficit in 1996 was 2.125 billion crowns.
Overall exports for January were stagnant at 20.588 billion crowns, just 0.9 percent more than in January 1996. Imports were 27.649 billion crowns, 22.3 percent higher year-on-year.

Analysts said the figures showed a continued widening trend for the deficit, but added it is still too early to draw any firm conclusions on whether recent central bank moves are helping slow imports, improving the overall balance.

"The latest central bank moves aimed at curbing a higher domestic demand, and thus the widening trade deficit, only took effect January 1, and any the effect of measures take a while to show," Juraj Rencko, Forecasting Institute Director with Slovak Academy of Science, told Reuters.
"A solution to the widening trade deficit is an adjustment of the economy's growth rate to (increase) its export efficiency," he added.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) set new rules at the beginning of the year for foreign exchange positions for monetary purposes -- and penalties for breaching the measures -- in an attempt to reduce the sector's rapid loan expansion which had helped fuel a consumption boom, spurring imports.
At the heart of January's deficit increase were imports of fossil fuels and mineral oils, accounting for 5.563 billion crowns, a year-on-year increase of 32.94 percent, SUSR said.

Imports of technology for the upgrading of the ageing Jaslovske Bohunice nuclear power plant and for the completion of the Mochovce nuclear power plant totalled 4.78 billion crowns in January, a rise of 63.28 percent year-on-year.
The fastest growth in exports was that of various types of motor vehicles, rising 86.79 percent year-on-year, and accounting for 2.069 billion crowns.
Exports of iron and rolled steel, dipped to 3.39 billion crowns for the month, a year-on-year decrease of 2.14 percent.
The Czech Republic remained Slovakia's leading trading partner, accounting for 22 percent of overall imports, and was the destination for 28.4 percent of all of Slovakia's exports.
Germany followed with a 26.2 share in Slovak exports and was in third place in imports, accounting for 15.3 percent.
Imports from Russia accounted for 19.6 percent, and were 1.413 billion crowns, 35.2 percent, higher year-on- year.
Slovak exports to the Russian Federation fell by 404 million crowns, or 57.7 percent, compared with January 1996.
Earlier in February, the Slovak parliament approved a law creating a state Export-Import bank to help boost exports and curb a burgeoning foreign trade deficit.
The bank, expected to begin operation sometime later this year, will be wholly state-owned and start with a basic capital of two billion crowns, all of which will come from the 1997 state budget.
